title: Why async: I/O versus blocking (freeing threads during waits)
hook: A blocked thread waiting on a network call is paid-for capacity doing nothing. The async and await keywords let that thread serve other work while the network is still thinking.

blocks.text: Asynchronous programming in C# is about waiting efficiently. When your code calls an HTTP endpoint, reads from a queue, or waits on a database, most of the time is spent off the CPU — the network or disk is still working. A blocking call holds a thread-pool thread for the entire wait. async and await let the thread return to the pool so other messages or requests can start. This is not parallelism — it is concurrency. One cook starting toast and moving to eggs is async. Two cooks is parallel.

entries.plainDefinition: Operations that spend most of their time waiting on external systems — network, disk, database.
entries.example: await httpClient.GetAsync(url) — the CPU is idle while the response travels.

entries.plainDefinition: Operations that keep the processor busy — hashing, image processing, sorting large lists.
entries.example: Computing a hash of a 10 MB file — async does not make this faster.

entries.plainDefinition: A synchronous call that holds the calling thread until it completes.
entries.example: .GetAwaiter().GetResult() on an async HTTP call blocks the thread.

entries.plainDefinition: A shared set of worker threads the .NET runtime manages. Blocking calls waste pool threads.
entries.example: ASP.NET Core and background workers both use the thread pool.

blocks.text: In a .NET worker processing queue messages, blocking Receive holds a thread-pool thread for seconds. Under high concurrency, you starve the pool before the CPU is busy — requests queue up with idle processors. await registers a continuation and releases the thread. Throughput is about concurrent in-flight I/O, not spinning more threads. CPU-bound work such as image rasterization is a different problem — it belongs in Task.Run or a dedicated pipeline, not in the async keyword itself.

blocks.title: When interviewers ask why not just use more threads
blocks.body: Say: "Threads are expensive — each has a stack and scheduling overhead. async frees threads during I/O waits so the same cores can start more waits. For CPU work, you need actual parallelism, which is a separate decision."

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Start an I/O operation
items.body: Call an async API like ReceiveMessageAsync or GetAsync.

items.title: Blocking path
items.body: GetResult() or .Wait() holds the thread until the response arrives. No other work on that thread.

items.title: Async path
items.body: await registers a continuation callback and returns the thread to the pool immediately.

items.title: Completion
items.body: When I/O finishes, a pool thread picks up the continuation and resumes your method.

snippet.label: Blocking receive versus awaited receive
snippet.explanation: GetResult holds the worker thread until SQS answers. await registers a continuation and releases the thread for other polls.

snippet.label: Start independent I/O, then compose
snippet.explanation: Awaiting A then B is still A plus B wall-clock time. Starting both then WhenAll overlaps the waits. This is concurrent I/O, not parallel CPU.

snippet.label: Task.Run does not make blocking I/O async
snippet.explanation: Task.Run queues CPU work to the pool. Wrapping a blocking call hides the blocking from the reader but still wastes a thread for the wait.

snippet.label: Diagnose thread-pool starvation
snippet.explanation: How to prove it in production: rising queue length with low CPU is the starvation signature. Async keeps queue depth flat under the same load.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling .Result or .Wait() on async I/O in a library used by ASP.NET Core. Assuming async methods run in parallel on multiple cores. Using Task.Run to wrap a blocking receive and calling that async. Confusing async (compose waits) with parallelism (use multiple cores).

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: under load test, compare throughput of blocking ReceiveMessage versus ReceiveMessageAsync at equal concurrency. dotnet-counters ThreadPool QueueLength climbs with blocking; async keeps it flat. CPU utilization staying below 30% while requests queue is the signature of thread starvation, not CPU saturation. The correct metric is concurrent in-flight I/O operations, not thread count.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Correct for CPU-bound, wrong for I/O

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'async makes code faster' — it makes concurrency cheaper, not individual operations faster. Claiming async uses multiple cores for a single sequential await chain. Using Task.Run to wrap blocking I/O and calling it 'async' — you still waste a thread. Not knowing the difference between concurrent I/O (one thread, many waits) and parallel CPU (many threads).

interviewTakeaways: async/await frees threads during I/O waits — it is a scalability tool, not a CPU speed-up.
Blocking .Result on pool threads causes starvation: requests queue while CPUs sit idle.
In production, dotnet-counters ThreadPool QueueLength rising with low CPU means blocking, not CPU saturation.
60s: async is for I/O wait. await releases the thread. Blocking holds a pool thread for the entire wait. WhenAll overlaps independent I/O. Task.Run is for CPU, not I/O. Measure with dotnet-counters.
Follow-up: how many concurrent SQS receives can one thread handle with async versus blocking?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'async makes things faster' gets you rejected — it improves concurrency, not per-operation latency.
Calling .Result on async I/O in a library — works in tests, starves the pool in production.
Strong answer: 'async frees threads during I/O. Blocking caps throughput at pool size. I use WhenAll for independent I/O and diagnose starvation with dotnet-counters.'

jsTsCorrelations.concept: Non-blocking I/O on a single thread
jsTsCorrelations.note: Node's event loop also frees the JS thread during I/O. C# await does the same for a pool thread. Neither turns CPU-heavy work into free concurrency.
await Promise.all([a, b]) on one JS thread overlaps I/O like Task.WhenAll on one pool thread. Both are concurrent waits, not parallel CPU execution.
